title: Raga kirtan today
hook: the raga name at the top of each hymn is like a recipe card, and teachers and ragis still cook from it, alongside simpler tunes

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ragmala, the garland of raga names on the Granth's last printed page, and two ways of reading it. Your line was differ with respect. Where did you keep sitting at the table? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-nine.

A recipe card, soft at the corners, in a grandmother's handwriting. The measurements are vague. A handful. Enough. Until it smells right. The card alone can't make the dish. Somebody has to have stood next to her at the stove. And yet as long as someone keeps cooking from it, the card stays alive. For weeks now, every hymn we've opened has come with a raga name at the top, like the title on that card. Today: who is still cooking from it.
screen: `A RECIPE CARD, SOFT AT THE CORNERS.` → `THE CARD ALONE CAN'T MAKE THE DISH.` → `WHO STILL COOKS FROM IT?`

segments.voice: Start with what's on the page. The Granth gathers its hymns under raga headings: Sri Rag, Majh, Gauri, and on through Kalyan, Prabhati and Jaijavanti. The heading tells the singer the musical mode the hymn is set in. The text doesn't write out a melody note by note. Like the grandmother's card, it names the dish and trusts that someone knows how to cook it. That knowing lives in people. In the gurdwara, the singers of kirtan are called ragis, and their craft is passed from teacher to student, voice to voice. Some ragis and teachers give their lives to singing each shabad in the raga its heading names, often with stringed instruments as well as harmonium and tabla. This way of singing is often called Gurmat Sangeet, the music of the Guru's way, and there are schools and teachers devoted to keeping it. Alongside it, in other gurdwaras and homes, shabads are sung to simpler tunes, easy for a whole congregation to pick up, sometimes with a repeated refrain everyone joins. Sikhs hold different views about how closely kirtan should follow the named raga, and the singing goes on in both ways, sometimes in the same building on the same day. What both share is the text. The Sikh Rehat Maryada, in paraphrase, says that in the congregation kirtan is the singing of Gurbani, with only certain other writings allowed beside it. The words don't change. The tune is the part handed down by ear. So the raga names we've walked through this block aren't museum labels. Somewhere a student may be learning Prabhati for a morning program, and a ragi tuning up for Kalyan at dusk. Your line: the old tunes live.
screen: `THE HEADING NAMES THE RAGA.` · `RAGIS: TEACHER TO STUDENT.` · `RAGA KIRTAN AND SIMPLER TUNES.` · `THE WORDS STAY; THE TUNE IS HANDED DOWN.` · then, large: `THE OLD TUNES LIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find a raga-based recording. If you can, search for one shabad sung in the raga its heading names; adding the words raag kirtan or Gurmat Sangeet to the search will often turn one up. Play it, and as it starts, sit still. For two minutes, don't try to analyze the music. Just notice how the voice and the instruments move together, rising and settling. Let the breath follow the music's pace instead of your own. If you can't play anything, sit in the quiet and recall any melody you learned from a person rather than a screen. If you pray, you can listen as kirtan is meant to be heard, as Gurbani sung. If you don't, simply listen like someone being taught. The bell holds the time.
Raga kirtan today. Shabads sung in the raga named at the top of the hymn, kept alive by ragis, teachers and schools, alongside simpler congregational tunes. Today's word.
Your line: the old tunes live. Today, ask someone older than you for a song, a recipe or a saying they learned by ear, and let them teach it to you. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-nine.
